quests.explanation: From Latin 'mater' (mother) and Greek 'archein' (to rule), a matriarch is the female head who 'rules' or leads a family.
Compare this to 'matriarch' — 'patri' relates to 'father,' describing the male head of a family or group.
From Latin 'extraneus' (foreign), estrangement describes becoming emotionally distant, almost like a 'stranger,' from someone close.
The prefix 're-' means 'again,' so reconciliation is the process of bringing people back together 'again' after a conflict.
Originally referring to tools ('loom' equipment) passed down to an 'heir,' this word now describes any treasured family object handed down.
The suffix '-age' turns 'line' (as in family line) into a noun describing your ancestry traced back through generations.
The prefix 'dys-' means 'bad' or 'abnormal,' so a dysfunctional family or system isn't working the way it normally should.
The prefix 'co-' means 'together,' so cohabitation describes two people living 'together' in the same home.
This transparent compound word describes someone who 'gives care' to another person, often a family member.
Unlike 'assistant' or 'consultant,' which use '-ant,' the word 'dependent' uses the '-ent' ending — a frequent point of confusion.
From Greek 'derma' (skin), a dermatologist is a doctor specializing in conditions of the skin.
From Greek 'ophthalmos' (eye), this word keeps an unusual 'phth' cluster that's one of the hardest in English to spell correctly.
From Greek 'orthos' (straight) and 'odous' (tooth), an orthodontist straightens teeth, often with braces.
From Latin 'claustrum' (enclosed place) and Greek 'phobos' (fear), claustrophobia is a fear of confined spaces.
From Greek 'hypo-' (under) and 'chondros' (cartilage, near the ribs), this term originally described anxiety believed to start near the ribs.
The suffix '-ance' turns the verb 'clear' (to remove) into a noun describing a sale meant to 'clear' out old stock.
Sharing a root with 'merchant,' this word describes goods bought and sold, ending in the less common '-dise' rather than '-dize.'
This compound word describes a 'house' (building) for storing 'wares' (goods) before they're sold or shipped.
Borrowed from French, 'boutique' keeps the original 'que' ending pronounced 'k,' unlike typical English spelling patterns.
This compound word describes selling goods as a 'whole' (in bulk) rather than individually to single customers.

quests.hint: Remember it's spelled with one 'l' in American English: IN-STALL-MENT.
quests.explanation: American English spells this 'installment' with one 'l' after 'stall,' while British English uses 'instalment' with a different pattern.
From French 'rembourser' (to repay), reimbursement describes money paid back to cover an expense you already paid.
The suffix '-ize' turns the noun 'item' into a verb meaning to list things individually, as on a detailed receipt.
The prefix 'non-' simply negates 'refundable,' describing a purchase that cannot be returned for money back.
From Latin 'consignare' (to seal together), consignment describes goods given to a seller who pays the owner only after the item sells.
This compound word describes having 'too much stock,' more than a store can easily sell.
From Latin 'liquidus' (fluid), liquidation describes turning assets into cash, as if making them 'fluid' again.
From Old French 'franchir' (to free), a franchise originally meant a special privilege or freedom, now describing a licensed business model.
From Greek 'monos' (single) and 'polein' (to sell), a monopoly exists when a 'single' seller controls an entire market.
From Latin 'glomus' (ball or mass), a conglomerate is many separate companies gathered 'together' into one large mass.
